claims.claim: Robinovitch and colleagues analysed 227 falls from 130 residents, captured on video between 2007 and 2010 in two long-term care facilities in British Columbia, Canada.
claims.supporting_passage: We did this observational study between April 20, 2007, and June 23, 2010, in two long-term care facilities in British Columbia, Canada. Digital video cameras were installed in common areas (dining rooms, lounges, hallways). ... We captured 227 falls from 130 individuals (mean age 78 years, SD 10).
claims.location: Abstract, Methods and Findings
claims.pico_timeframe: Residents of two long-term care facilities / video-captured falls in common areas / no comparator / cause of imbalance and activity at time of fall / April 2007 to June 2010
claims.safe_wording: Researchers filmed 227 falls by 130 residents of two care homes in British Columbia, Canada, between 2007 and 2010.
claims.qualifications: Say 'care homes' (long-term care facilities); say cameras were in shared areas only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None for the descriptive facts.

numbers.meaning: all video-captured falls analysed, 2007 to 2010
people whose falls were captured; mean age 78
long-term care facilities in British Columbia, Canada

claims.claim: The commonest cause of falling was incorrect shifting of body weight (41%); trips or stumbles caused 21% and slips only 3%.
claims.supporting_passage: The most frequent cause of falling was incorrect weight shifting, which accounted for 41% (93 of 227) of falls, followed by trip or stumble (48, 21%), hit or bump (25, 11%), loss of support (25, 11%), and collapse (24, 11%). Slipping accounted for only 3% (six) of falls.
claims.location: Abstract, Findings
claims.pico_timeframe: 227 video-captured falls / cause of imbalance rated by a team with a validated questionnaire
claims.safe_wording: About 4 in 10 of the filmed falls (93 of 227) came from shifting body weight the wrong way during an ordinary movement. About 1 in 5 (48) came from a trip or stumble, and 6 from a slip.
claims.qualifications: These are shares of falls filmed in shared areas, not of all falls in the homes. Causes were judged by a research team watching the videos.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors note self-report studies found different patterns; they attribute part of the difference to location (their data exclude bedrooms and bathrooms). Do not say 'most falls did not involve an obstacle': hit or bump (11%) and loss of support from an object (11%) also involve external objects. It is accurate that trips and slips together were about 1 in 4 (54 of 227).

numbers.meaning: incorrect weight shifting, share of filmed falls
trip or stumble
hit or bump; loss of support; collapse
slip

claims.claim: Falls happened most often during forward walking, standing quietly and sitting down; about a fifth happened during transfers.
claims.supporting_passage: The three activities associated with the highest proportion of falls were forward walking (54 of 227 falls, 24%), standing quietly (29 falls, 13%), and sitting down (28 falls, 12%). Compared with previous reports from the long-term care setting, we identified a higher occurrence of falls during standing and transferring, a lower occurrence during walking ... 21% of falls occurred during transferring, suggesting the need for exercises to enhance muscle strength, and improved assistive devices that provide adequate body support (eg, locking of wheels) when moving to and from chairs. ... The activities associated with fewest falls were standing and reaching, standing and turning, and seated or wheeling in a wheelchair (table 4).
claims.location: Abstract, Findings; Results; Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: 227 filmed falls / activity at time of fall
claims.safe_wording: The commonest moments were walking forward (54 falls), standing still (29) and sitting down (28). About 1 in 5 falls happened while moving to or from a chair or bed.
claims.qualifications: Do not list turning as a common moment: standing and turning was among the activities with the fewest falls. These are counts of falls, not risk per minute spent on each activity (the study did not measure time spent in each activity).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Proportions by activity partly reflect how often residents do each activity.

numbers.meaning: falls during forward walking
falls while standing quietly
falls while sitting down
falls during transferring (authors' Discussion)

claims.claim: Cameras were only in common areas, not bedrooms or bathrooms, so the findings describe falls in shared spaces.
claims.supporting_passage: Digital video cameras were installed in common areas (dining rooms, lounges, hallways); Delta View had a network of 216 cameras, and New Vista had 48. No cameras were located in bedrooms or bathrooms. ... In 2010, at Delta View, 45% of falls documented on incident report occurred in common areas, of which 65% were captured on video. At New Vista, 34% of documented falls occurred in common areas, of which 28% were captured on video. ... We did not measure (and were unable to incorporate in a risk analysis) the amount of time spent doing the various activities associated with falls. ... We stress that our results summarise the situational context of falls in common areas of the long-term care environment.
claims.location: Methods, Procedures; Results; Discussion (limitations)
claims.pico_timeframe: Two facilities; 2010 incident-report comparison
claims.safe_wording: The cameras were in lounges, dining rooms and corridors only. Falls in bedrooms and bathrooms, where many care home falls happen, were not filmed.
claims.qualifications: Put this limitation on the chart itself. Do not state what share of all care home falls happen in bedrooms; the paper gives only that 45% and 34% of documented falls at the two sites were in common areas in 2010.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors report that people with filmed falls had similar demographics to those whose falls were not filmed (January to June 2010).

numbers.meaning: share of incident-reported falls in 2010 that occurred in common areas, at the two facilities
share of those common-area falls that were captured on video in 2010

claims.claim: Falls prevention in care homes should give as much attention to transfers and sitting down as to trip hazards.
claims.supporting_passage: Our findings emphasise the need to target each of these activities in fall risk assessment and prevention strategies. ... We showed that 25% of trips occurred due to the foot being caught on a chair or table leg, suggesting the need for improved staff awareness of this hazard, and improvements in environmental planning and furniture design. 21% of falls occurred during transferring, suggesting the need for exercises to enhance muscle strength, and improved assistive devices that provide adequate body support (eg, locking of wheels) when moving to and from chairs.
claims.location: Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Authors' interpretation; no intervention tested
claims.safe_wording: The authors suggested strength exercise and better support when moving to and from chairs, and noted that a quarter of trips were over chair or table legs. We should give sitting down, standing up and transfers the same attention as clearing trip hazards.
claims.qualifications: Mark the position as judgement drawn from the finding ('We should...'), not a tested intervention. Keep the furniture-leg point so the post does not dismiss trip hazards.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial in this study showed that focusing on transfers reduces falls.

numbers.meaning: trips where the foot caught on a chair or table leg (share of the 48 trips)

claims.claim: Repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years of onset are a core feature (P1, highest certainty level) in the MDS criteria for progressive supranuclear palsy; 'backward' falls are not part of the criterion wording.
claims.supporting_passage: Table 2, Postural instability, Level 1: "P1: Repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years". Table 4 definition: "Spontaneous loss of balance while standing, or history of more than one unprovoked fall, within 3 years after onset of PSP-related features." Discussion: "We are also aware of several other clinical signs that have been proposed to indicate the diagnosis of PSP, for example, retropulsion with spontaneous backward falls ... Whereas these signs may indeed be helpful to raise suspicion about PSP, we found no clear evidence suggesting that they would indeed contribute reliable information to substantiate the diagnosis of PSP." Table 5: Probable PSP = "(O1 or O2) + (P1 or P2)", "PSP with Richardson's syndrome".
claims.location: Tables 2, 4 and 5; Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Diagnostic criteria; falls within 3 years after onset of PSP-related features
claims.safe_wording: In the Movement Disorder Society criteria for progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years of the first symptoms are a core feature. Combined with slowed or restricted up-and-down eye movements, they support a diagnosis of probable PSP.
claims.qualifications: Carousel label: 'Repeated falls without a clear cause in the first 3 years: think PSP'. Do not write 'early backward falls: think PSP' as if it were the criterion; backward falls are a traditional sign that the criteria authors found no clear evidence for.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Falls alone do not make the diagnosis; the criteria combine falls with eye-movement signs.

numbers.meaning: time window after onset of PSP-related features
unprovoked falls needed for P1 (or spontaneous loss of balance while standing)

claims.claim: Recurrent falls due to impaired balance within 3 years of onset are a red flag against Parkinson's disease in the 2015 MDS criteria, and in autopsy-confirmed cases they were documented far less often in PD than in atypical parkinsonism.
claims.supporting_passage: Red Flags were described as negative features which are potential signs of alternate pathology, but with lower or uncertain specificity. Red Flags rule out probable PD only when they cannot be counterbalanced by supportive criteria ... Table 1: "Recurrent falls (>1 per year) within first 3 years". Results: "'Recurrent falling because of impaired balance within 3 y' was reported in 3.8% of 124 PD cases and 28% in 19 DLB cases. In 274 MSA cases, these early falls were reported in 28.8%, in 33.6% of 28 PSP cases and in 22% of 27 CBD cases." Discussion: "Items with less clear discriminative value were 'rapid progression of gait impairment', 'recurrent falls', and 'bilateral symmetric Parkinsonism', as these features were reported in 3.8–17.6% of PD cases."
claims.location: Introduction; Table 1; Results, Red Flags; Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Autopsy-confirmed PD and atypical parkinsonism from 28 clinicopathological series, 1988 to 2024 / documented early recurrent falls
claims.safe_wording: Repeated falls from poor balance in the first 3 years of a Parkinson-like illness are a warning sign in the Movement Disorder Society criteria that the illness may be something other than Parkinson's disease. In people whose diagnosis was confirmed after death, such early falls were recorded in about 4 in 100 with Parkinson's disease and about 1 in 3 with PSP.
claims.qualifications: A red flag, not an exclusion: it can be outweighed by features supporting PD. Autopsy numbers are small for PSP (28 cases) and come from retrospective notes. The same review advises making sure dopamine treatment is adequate before relying on early falls as a red flag.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: About two thirds of the PSP cases in this dataset had no early recurrent falls documented, so absence of early falls does not rule PSP out. Postuma 2015 (the original criteria) could not be opened; the wording comes from this 2025 review.

numbers.meaning: autopsy-confirmed PD cases with documented recurrent falls within 3 years
autopsy-confirmed PSP cases with such falls
MSA cases
DLB and CBD cases

When changing directions, steps are small and unstable. ... pathological gait features, such as small-step gait (short length of stride), broad-based gait (increasingly large step intervals), instability, difficulty in changing directions, frozen gait (no first step taken), and shuffle (dragging of feet and decreased elevation)
claims.location: Chapter 1, Characteristics and evaluation of gait disturbance; Chapter 3, CSF drainage test
claims.pico_timeframe: Guideline description of iNPH gait
claims.safe_wording: Normal pressure hydrocephalus typically causes short, wide-based steps with the feet barely lifted, which become more unsteady on turning.

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The guideline notes some features overlap with Parkinson's disease (freezing), but external cues help less in NPH.

Meanwhile, a large-scale questionnaire survey conducted in Japan in 2012 revealed that the full triad was present in only 12.1% of 1524 patients. ... Urge incontinence associated with an overactive bladder is characteristic of dysuria in patients with iNPH.

claims.qualifications: Do not imply urgency and slowed thinking must be present before NPH is considered.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Triad completeness ranges from about 60% in hospital series to 12.1% in a national survey.

claims.claim: Shunt surgery is effective for NPH and many people improve, with walking improving most.
claims.supporting_passage: CSF shunt intervention is effective for treating iNPH. Recommendation Grade 1, Level of Evidence B ... Symptoms usually improve after surgical intervention. ... The degree of improvement in gait disturbance is the highest, followed by cognitive impairment and urinary dysfunction. ... Based on evaluations such as mRS, improvement rate after shunt intervention is reported to be approximately 39–81% in 3–6 months, 63–84% in 1 year, 69% in 2 years, and approximately 60–74% in 3–6 years. ... gait disturbance showed the highest rate of improvement ... approximately 60–77%.

claims.claim: Marked unsteadiness with eyes closed (a positive Romberg test) points to loss of position sense, for example from neuropathy, but also occurs with loss of inner-ear balance function; it is not a test of cerebellar function.
claims.supporting_passage: In clinical neurology, the Romberg test is traditionally used to assess postural stability by altering visual input, thereby unmasking disequilibrium in patients with sensory ataxia caused by proprioceptive deficits. ... The classic Romberg test primarily evaluates proprioceptive function, particularly the integrity of the posterior columns of the spinal cord. ... It is not a test of cerebellar function, as cerebellar dysfunction typically leads to balance impairment regardless of visual input. ... While the Romberg test is standard, it fails to clearly differentiate vestibular from sensory ataxia. (Anagnostou 2025) / ... sensory ataxia, as both conditions typically present with a positive classical Romberg test. (Anagnostou 2025 abstract) / We conclude that the Romberg test ... had an unsatisfactory classification value in terms of distinguishing patients from healthy controls. Instead, it should be interpreted within the comprehensive context of the broader neurological examination and the electrodiagnosis of peripheral nerve function. (Anagnostou 2024 abstract)
claims.location: Anagnostou 2025 Abstract and Introduction; Anagnostou 2024 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Bedside test physiology; small posturography studies
claims.safe_wording: If someone is much more unsteady standing with eyes closed than open, they are relying on vision to balance. Think of loss of position sense in the feet and legs (for example from neuropathy) or loss of inner-ear balance function.
claims.qualifications: Carousel label: 'Much worse with eyes closed: think loss of position sense (for example neuropathy) or inner-ear balance loss'. The test is a pointer, to be read with the rest of the examination.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Quantified Romberg testing separated neuropathy patients from controls only modestly (Anagnostou 2024).

claims.claim: In a 1997 study of 58 residents of sheltered accommodation in Umea, Sweden, 10 of the 12 who stopped walking when a conversation started fell within 6 months, compared with 11 of the 46 who kept walking.

The staff registered falls indoors during a followup of 6 months. ... 12 people stopped walking when a conversation started and ten of them fell during the 6-month follow-up. 21 people fell at least once. ... The positive predictive value of “stops walking when talking” was 83% (10/12) and the negative predictive value was 76% (35/46). (Lundin-Olsson 1997, letter text) / Lundin-Olsson and colleagues12 13 reported that this test demonstrated good specificity (95%) as well as acceptable positive predictive values (PPV, 83%) and negative predictive values (NPV, 76%) with moderate sensitivity (48%) in predicting falls. claims.claim: Stopping walking when talking was highly specific but insensitive for later falls: most people who fell had kept walking.
claims.supporting_passage: The specificity was high (95%; 35/37) but the sensitivity was low (48%; 10/21). (Lundin-Olsson 1997 letter text) / Lundin-Olsson and colleagues12 13 reported that this test demonstrated good specificity (95%) ... with moderate sensitivity (48%) in predicting falls. (Hyndman 2004) / The pooled odds ratio for falling was 5.3 (95% CI, 3.1-9.1) when subjects had changes in gait or attention-demanding task performance whilst dual tasking. ... The predictive value for falling was particularly efficient amongst frail older adults compared with healthy subjects. Two prospective studies challenged the usefulness of the dual-task paradigm as a significant predictor compared to single task performance and three studies even reported that gait changes whilst dual tasking did not predict falls. (Beauchet 2009 abstract)

claims.safe_wording: In that study, only 2 of the 37 people who did not fall had stopped walking, so the sign was rarely a false alarm. But 11 of the 21 people who fell had kept walking, so its absence was weak reassurance.
claims.qualifications: The specific-but-insensitive finding comes from the original 1997 study itself. Do not attribute 'high specificity, low sensitivity' to the Beauchet 2009 review: its abstract reports that dual-task changes in general were linked with falls (pooled odds ratio 5.3), especially in frail people, and does not give sensitivity or specificity for the sign.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Beauchet found conflicting studies (3 found no prediction). Do not convert the pooled odds ratio into 'five times more likely'.

claims.claim: In nursing and residential care, providing hip protectors probably reduces hip fractures slightly: about 11 fewer people per 1000 (from about 60 to about 49 per 1000 over about a year).
claims.supporting_passage: Pooling of data from 14 studies (11,808 participants) conducted in nursing or residential care settings found moderate quality evidence for a small reduction in hip fracture risk (risk ratio (RR) 0.82, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.67 to 1.00); the absolute effect is 11 fewer people (95% CI, from 20 fewer to 0) per 1000 having a hip fracture when provided with hip protectors. / Summary of findings: Hip fractures at 1 year older people living in institutions, Follow-up: 6-24 months; No hip protectors provided: Moderate risk 60 per 1000; Hip protectors provided: 49 per 1000 (40 to 60); RR 0.82 (0.67 to 1.00); 11808 (14 studies); moderate. / Plain language summary: In older people living in nursing care facilities, providing a hip protector - probably decreases the chance of a hip fracture slightly
claims.location: Abstract, Main results; Summary of findings table 1; Plain language summary
claims.pico_timeframe: Residents of nursing or residential care / provided with hip protectors / not provided / hip fracture / about 1 year (trials 6 to 24 months)
claims.safe_wording: In care homes, offering hip protectors probably prevents a small number of hip fractures. Over about a year, roughly 60 in every 1000 residents without them would break a hip, compared with about 49 in 1000 offered them: about 11 fewer.
claims.qualifications: The effect is of offering protectors (intention to treat), not of wearing them. The 60 per 1000 is the review's assumed baseline risk. The range runs from about 20 fewer to no difference, so the benefit could be very small. Moderate certainty.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Kiel 2007, a large US nursing home trial with good adherence, found no protective effect (hip fracture 3.1% on protected hips versus 2.5% on unprotected hips). Kannus 2000 found a large effect (21.3 versus 46.0 hip fractures per 1000 person-years). A 2024 umbrella review (Da 2024) agrees in direction; do not quote its relative risk alongside the Cochrane figure.

Overall adherence was 73.8%. (Kiel 2007) / In the hip-protector group, four subjects had a hip fracture (among 1034 falls) while wearing the protector, and nine subjects had a hip fracture (among 370 falls) while not wearing the protector (Kannus 2000)

candidates.reason: All the study facts and numbers are verified in the full text (227 falls, 130 residents, 41% weight shifting, 21% trips, 3% slips, walking 24%, standing 13%, sitting down 12%, cameras only in common areas). 'Most filmed falls did not involve the floor or an obstacle' is too loose, because hit or bump and loss of support also involve objects. candidates.revised_angle: Filmed falls in two Canadian care homes: about 4 in 10 came from shifting weight the wrong way during ordinary movement, and trips and slips together caused about 1 in 4. The commonest moments were walking, standing still and sitting down, and about 1 in 5 happened during transfers. We should give sitting down, standing up and transfers as much attention as trip hazards (judgement). State on the chart that cameras were in shared areas only and that the counts are not risk per activity.

candidates.reason: Every vignette can be supported, but the draft labels need changing. The PSP criterion is 'repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years', not 'early backward falls'; backward falls are a traditional sign the criteria authors found no clear evidence for. The PD red flag (Postuma 2015) could not be opened; its wording and autopsy frequencies come from Fox 2025, which also shows early falls in 3.8% of PD and a third of PSP. For NPH, the post must not imply that urgency and slowed thinking are required. A positive Romberg also occurs with inner-ear balance loss. B12 is supported for neuropathy and cord damage, not for the Romberg sign directly. candidates.revised_angle: Falls as a symptom: three walking patterns that point to a named, sometimes treatable condition. (1) Repeated falls without a clear cause in the first 3 years of a Parkinson-like illness: think PSP, and question a Parkinson's diagnosis. (2) Short, wide-based steps, feet barely lifted, unsteady on turning, often with bladder urgency or slower thinking: think NPH, where selected people often improve after a shunt. (3) Much worse with eyes closed: think loss of position sense (for example neuropathy, including from B12 deficiency) or inner-ear balance loss. Close: watch every person who falls walk, turn and stand with eyes closed before blaming age.

candidates.reason: The 1997 figures are supported (58 residents; 10 of 12 who stopped walking fell within 6 months versus 11 of 46 who kept walking; specificity 95%, sensitivity 48%). The counts come from the Consensus reproduction of the letter and the percentages are also in the Hyndman 2004 full text. But the candidate credits 'high specificity, low sensitivity' to Beauchet 2009, and that abstract does not say this; the finding is the original study's own. Replication is mixed (stroke: specificity 70%, sensitivity 53%; Parkinson's: did not predict; healthy volunteers: rare and not linked with past falls). The post must say the sign has been tested mainly in small studies. Candidate claim c (dual-task gait) is contested between reviews and should be left out or given as background only.
candidates.revised_angle: Stopping walking to answer a question is a famous bedside sign that rests on a very small 1997 study: 10 of the 12 who stopped fell within 6 months. In that study it was rarely a false alarm, but most people who fell had kept walking. Later studies in people with stroke, Parkinson's disease and healthy volunteers found it weaker. Plain rule: a positive sign means look harder with a full falls assessment; a negative sign does not reassure.

candidates.reason: The Cochrane figures are verified: care homes 60 versus 49 hip fractures per 1000 at about 1 year (11 fewer, range 20 fewer to 0, RR 0.82, moderate certainty); community little or no effect (10 versus 12 per 1000). But the core insight's claim that the benefit is 'mostly among people who wear them consistently' is not established. The review did no pooled analysis by adherence, and the large HIP PRO trial found no benefit even with over 80% adherence. The pelvic fracture signal is low certainty and must be omitted or stated as uncertain. The evidenced barriers are discomfort, acute illness, staff shortages and staff beliefs; continence and dressing were not named in the sources opened.
candidates.revised_angle: Open with the absolute number: in care homes, offering hip protectors to 1000 residents for about a year probably means about 49 hip fractures instead of about 60. The benefit is small and uncertain in size, many residents stop wearing them, and one large trial found no benefit even among regular wearers. For people living at home, trials found little or no effect. Hip protectors are a reasonable offer for high-risk care home residents who find them comfortable, alongside falls prevention and bone treatment, not instead of them.

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported by opened sources. It is commoner with age; about 6 in 10 have a recent head injury recorded, so the knock is often minor or missing from the history. Symptoms appear over days to weeks, and it can present weeks or months after the bleed. Unsteadiness or falls (58.6%), headache, one-sided weakness, worse thinking and drowsiness are common. Required wording: 'often treatable', not 'treatable'; mention embolisation as an add-on to drainage from 2024 trials (2 of 3 positive); keep the thinking change described as slower thinking and not as delirium.
